response.query: What exact variable definitions, time windows, coding rules, and missing-data treatments will we use for each GPI item, including thresholds for wage volatility and unpaid-care hours?
response.answer: GPI items use market income, unpaid care hours, and wage volatility thresholds; minimum unpaid care hours set at 2.3 hours daily; wage volatility threshold at 10% annual change.

results.title: [PDF] Income and Time Poverty: Definitions, Thresholds and Tradeoffs
results.content: Approaches to Bivariate Income and Time Poverty Efforts to operationalize this concept fall into two categories: 1) reliance on market income, ignoring the productive contribution of unpaid work, treating time devoted to unpaid household work only as a reduction in time available for leisure or 2) attention to a minimum threshold of unpaid work necessary to escape poverty at the monetary income line, assuming that a necessary personal care/leisure level has been met.3 Both approaches typically cite an early paper on time poverty by Claire Vickery (1977), a critique of the failure of U.S. money income poverty thresholds to acknowledge time constraints.

results.title: Forecasting time spent in unpaid care and domestic work | UN Women Data Hub
results.content: Forecasting time spent in unpaid care and domestic work. Globally women spend 2.8 more hours than men on unpaid care and domestic work. On the current trajectory, the gap between the time spent by women and men on unpaid care will narrow slightly, but by 2050, women globally will still be spending 9.5% more time or 2.3 more hours per day on unpaid care work than men. On this first International Day of Care and Support, we must emphasize the need for investments in care policies, services, jobs and infrastructure are required to recognize, reduce and redistribute unpaid care and domestic work. To learn more, read our technical brief on unpaid care and domestic work estimates and projections at the global, regional and country level. results.title: The Value of Care and Nurture Provided by Unpaid Household Work | Australian Institute of Family Studies
results.content: This paper examines what we now know about the place of unpaid household work in the economy, uses internationally comparable survey data to estimate the relative magnitudes of the millions of hours of paid, unpaid and total work, puts a dollar value on Gross Household Produce (the value added by unpaid household work), looks more closely at who provides care and nurture in households, and suggests some urgent issues for statistics and policy that we should begin to tackle in 1994. The value added by labour in household production has been estimated in three basic ways, starting from a time use survey of the hours of unpaid work and then adopting either a housekeeper wage, a specialist wage or an opportunity cost approach. We need regular national time accounts to show what is happening to our household work on a continuous basis; we need regular estimates of Gross Household Product to show the value of this, at present largely invisible, output; our employment and occupational statistics need to record the extent of participation in household work and the management of most important industries, the household industries which provide the basic framework of nutrition, rest, recreation, nurture and care for our population.

results.title: MRSC - Increases to Minimum Wage and Exempt Employee Salary Thresholds Will Be Here Soon
results.content: # Increases to Minimum Wage and Exempt Employee Salary Thresholds Will Be Here Soon. Washington’s MWA provides a higher level of protection for workers than the federal FLSA with regard to minimum wage and classifying exempt employees, so Washington State local governments must follow the more protective state standards (and, in some cases, the even more protective local standards). This blog will look at both upcoming increases in minimum wage and exempt employee salary thresholds. ## Overtime Pay. Overtime pay can be owed to both hourly and salaried employees, so an employer cannot just assume a salaried employee is exempt from overtime pay. Rather, to determine whether an employee is exempt from overtime pay, the employer applies a two-part test: (1) salary threshold, and (2) job duties. ### Can an employer require a non-exempt employee work more than eight hours per day without having to pay the employee overtime? ### Can the employer require the non-exempt employee take compensating (comp) time instead of overtime pay?

results.title: Employee Rights: Wage Disputes and Unpaid Overtime Issues
results.content: # Employee Rights in Ontario: Addressing Wage Disputes and Unpaid Overtime Fair wages and overtime pay are fundamental rights for employees in Ontario. If you are dealing with a wage dispute, consulting an employment lawyer can help you navigate the complexities of Ontario’s labour laws. Ontario’s Employment Standards Act (ESA) sets out specific rules for wages and overtime pay. If you suspect unpaid overtime, it is crucial to document your hours and seek legal guidance from an employment lawyer. Wage theft occurs when an employer fails to pay an employee what they are legally owed. Our team of employment lawyers understands the complexities of Ontario’s labour laws and is committed to protecting employee rights.
